say: Read the two papers in Sources and summarize each in your own words, in a Notes folder: the problem it takes on, what it proposes, and what matters if we add real-time collaboration to our Markdown editor.

args.content:
**Source:** Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg, McGranaghan, "Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in spite of the Cloud", Onward! '19 (Sources/Local-first software)

## The problem

Cloud apps (Google Docs, Trello, Figma) gave us real-time collaboration and access from any device. The price is that the server holds the real copy of your data. If the service is slow, offline, changes its terms or shuts down, your work goes with it. Old-fashioned desktop apps that save files to disk give you ownership, speed and offline use, but collaborating with them means emailing files around, getting "conflicted copy" files, and merging by hand. The paper asks whether software can give users both.

## What it proposes

**Local-first software.** The copy on the user's device is the primary one. Servers keep secondary copies to help with sync and backup. The authors set out seven ideals:

1. **Fast.** Nothing waits on a server: reads and writes go to local storage, and sync happens in the background.
2. **Multi-device.** Data syncs across all of a user's devices.
3. **Offline.** Work goes on without a connection. Edits made offline sync later, possibly over a LAN or Bluetooth.
4. **Collaboration.** Real-time collaboration as good as the best cloud apps, plus async workflows such as suggestions and pull requests.
5. **Longevity.** The work stays readable and editable after the vendor is gone.
6. **Privacy.** No central store of everyone's data. End-to-end encryption, so servers hold only ciphertext.
7. **User control.** Users can copy, modify, back up or delete their data however they like.

They score existing approaches against these ideals: email attachments, web apps, Dropbox-style file sync, Git/GitHub, thin and thick clients, Firebase/CloudKit/Realm, CouchDB. None meets all seven. Git comes closest, but it has no real-time collaboration and works well only on line-based text.

Their candidate foundation is **CRDTs** (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types). These are ordinary-looking data structures (lists, maps, text) where every replica can be edited independently and any two replicas can be merged to the same result. CRDTs can sync over any channel: a server, peer-to-peer, or a USB stick. Changes can go out one keystroke at a time (live editing) or in batches (more like a pull request). The authors' library is **Automerge**.

## What their prototypes found

They built three Electron/React apps on Automerge: Trellis (Kanban board), PixelPusher (drawing) and PushPin (media canvas). Testing was informal: the five-person team plus about ten outside users.

- **CRDTs worked.** Automerge was reliable and easy to integrate, and merges were almost always seamless.
- **Offline use felt great.** You could work disconnected for as long as you liked and merge on reconnect.
- **React-style FRP suits CRDTs.** All state changes go through one reducer, so local and remote edits update the view the same way. Real-time and offline support came "with little effort".
- **Conflicts were rarer than feared.** Two reasons: merging works at a fine grain and knows the datatype, and people naturally avoid editing the same thing at the same time. Real conflicts arise only when two people change one field of one object at the same moment. Automerge's default resolution policies were enough in every prototype.
- **Showing history matters.** Changes can arrive at any moment from anyone, so users need a way to see how the document got to its current state. Trellis experimented with a "time travel" view.
- **URLs work well for sharing.** Permissions beyond "secret URL" are an open question.
- **Peer-to-peer state is hard to reason about.** No one is simply online or offline, and each user may see a different version.
- **History grows without limit.** CRDTs store every change, down to single keystrokes. This caused performance, memory and disk problems with real documents, and old history can't easily be dropped because a peer might reconnect months later.
- **Networking is unsolved.** P2P (WebRTC, Dat/Hypercore) was not production-ready, and NAT traversal was unreliable.
- **Servers still have a role, as "cloud peers".** They can relay documents between users who are never online at the same time (the "closed laptop" problem), store backups, bridge to other APIs, or provide burst compute. They support the system but are not the source of truth.

The authors' 2019 view was that Automerge was fine for prototypes but not yet a production replacement for something like Firebase.

## Open problems they name

- Branches, forks and the right to reject or hold back changes. Most CRDT work assumes everyone shares one live version.
- Schema and version compatibility when collaborators run different app versions and there is no central schema.
- UI for sync state, version history and change review. Is there anything better than diffs/patches or Docs-style suggestions?
- Permissions. What does "stop sharing" mean once someone has a copy?

## What matters for real-time collaboration in our Markdown editor

These are my readings of the paper, not its prescriptions.

- **Decide where the primary copy lives.** Local-first means the local document or file is authoritative and the server is a cloud peer. This affects offline behaviour, latency and how much users trust the app. Cloud-first is simpler but gives up most of the seven ideals.
- **Merge, don't lock.** Concurrent edits should merge automatically (CRDT, or OT for a server-centric design; the paper names ShareDB as an OT option). Turning conflicts into "conflicted copy" files is exactly the failure the paper describes.
- **Offline is the hard case.** Real-time collaboration is the easy path. The test is a long offline session followed by a merge.
- **Plan for history size.** Keystroke-level history grows quickly. We need compaction or an efficient storage format from the start.
- **Keep a relay server.** Pure P2P is fragile. A sync/relay server acting as a cloud peer solves "my collaborator was offline when I shared".
- **Show what changed.** Highlight incoming edits and keep some history view. Users need to see what others did.
- **Plain-text export is cheap longevity.** Markdown is already a durable format. Keep the `.md` file readable by other tools even if the collaboration state lives in a CRDT alongside it.
- **Open questions for us:** sharing and permissions, encryption on the server, and compatibility between app versions.

**Source:** Litt, Lim, Kleppmann, van Hardenberg, "Peritext: A CRDT for Collaborative Rich Text Editing", Proc. ACM HCI (CSCW2), 2022 (Sources/Peritext)

## The problem

Collaborative editing of plain text is well understood: there are many CRDTs for it. Rich text with formatting is not. The authors found no published rich-text CRDT, and they show that existing approaches produce results nobody intended:

- **Generic tree CRDT/OT (HTML/XML/JSON).** Formatting is modelled as deleting text and re-inserting it inside a new node. If one user bolds a word while another italicises it, the word gets **duplicated**. They observed this in Convergence.io + Froala.
- **OT-based editors** (Google Docs, CKEditor, ProseMirror, Quill) need a central server. They handle long offline periods badly and don't support branch-and-merge. CKEditor reportedly spent about 42 person-years on collaborative rich text.
- **Per-character attributes (Ritzy).** Text inserted into a span that is being bolded at the same time doesn't pick up the bold. A comment can be split in two by a concurrent insertion. Storing attributes on every character also costs memory.
- **Hidden start/end control characters (Yjs).** Overlapping bolds can cancel out. A concurrent unbold plus partial unbold can leave the **rest of the document bold**. The authors tried counting markers instead, and every fix broke another case. The underlying issue: markers show where formatting starts and ends, but not which formatting is newer.

## What it proposes

### 1. A specification of "intent preservation" for inline formatting

They give a set of two-user scenarios that work as a test suite:

- Text inserted inside a formatted span takes on that formatting, even if it was inserted concurrently.
- Overlapping bolds merge into one bold. Bold and italic overlapping gives both.
- Conflicting values (red vs blue, bold vs unbold on the same text) are settled by a deterministic **last-write-wins** rule, applied only where the spans overlap.
- Some marks can overlap: two comments on the same text are both kept.
- At span boundaries, new text inherits from the preceding character. That means bold/italic/colour **expand** when you type at their end, but **links and comments don't**. They checked this against Word, Google Docs and Pages.

These rules reduce to two settings per mark type:

| Mark | Overlaps itself | Grows when you type at its edge |
|---|---|---|
| Bold, italic, colour | No | Yes |
| Link | No | No |
| Comment | Yes | No |

The authors say the model is subjective: it keeps what each edit did, not what the writer meant by it. People will still fix up the meaning by hand.

### 2. The Peritext CRDT

- **The text is a plain-text CRDT** (RGA/Causal Trees). Every character has a unique, stable ID (a Lamport timestamp `counter@node`). Deleted characters remain as tombstones.
- **Formatting is stored separately from the text**, as an append-only set of `addMark` / `removeMark` operations. Each operation's start and end are anchored to character IDs, not positions. Every character has two anchor points, *before* and *after* it. Choosing which anchor a mark uses controls whether it expands: bold ends "before" the next character, so it grows when you type at its end; a link ends "after" its last character, so it doesn't.
- **Applying operations.** "Op-sets" are stored only at anchors where formatting changes, and applying a mark touches only the span it covers. They prove this is commutative: every replica converges whatever order operations arrive in.
- **Rendering.** For each span, the op-set is reduced to the current formatting: highest opId wins for exclusive marks, and all comments that haven't been removed are kept.
- **Incremental patches.** Each operation also produces index-based patches for the editor UI, so a keystroke doesn't trigger re-rendering the whole document.
- **Edge cases handled:** inserting at the start of a paragraph, and inserting next to tombstones at a link boundary.

### 3. Implementation and evaluation

- TypeScript prototype on a simplified Automerge, with a **ProseMirror** editor UI.
- Randomised property-based tests: 5,000+ operation traces across three peers, with no convergence failures.
- Formal convergence proof in the appendix.

## Limits the authors state

- **Inline formatting only.** No headings, lists, block quotes or tables, and no splitting, joining or moving blocks. That is left for future work.
- No diff or version visualisation yet, and no UI for flagging conflicts.
- Moving or cut-pasting text concurrently is unsolved.
- Storage grows without limit as written (tombstones plus full mark history). Their mitigations: store only the latest value per mark type, garbage-collect tombstones, use a tombstone-free CRDT, or use Automerge's compressed format (under 1 byte per operation).
- The prototype supports only bold, italic, links and comments.

## What matters for real-time collaboration in our Markdown editor

These are my readings; some depend on how our editor stores documents, which I haven't confirmed.

- **First question: what is the shared document, the Markdown source or a rich-text model?**
  - *If we sync the raw `.md` text* with a plain-text CRDT, Peritext isn't needed. But formatting then lives as inline syntax (`**`, `_`, `[...](...)`), and that is close to the control-character approach the paper shows failing. Two users bolding overlapping ranges at the same time could produce mismatched or nested `**` markers that render wrongly. Users can see and fix these, which helps, but they'll happen. *(My inference, not tested in the paper.)*
  - *If we sync a structured model* (e.g. a ProseMirror doc that serialises to Markdown), Peritext's approach of marks anchored to character IDs applies directly to emphasis, strong, code, links and comments.
- **Markdown is mostly blocks**: headings, lists, quotes, code fences, tables. Peritext doesn't cover them, so either way we need a separate answer for concurrent block edits (split, join, reorder, nest).
- **Use the overlap/expand table** to configure each mark we support. Strong and emphasis expand. Links and comments don't. Inline code is our decision.
- **Comments as non-expanding, overlapping marks** anchored to character IDs, with comment content in a separate store. This is a clean model if we add review comments.
- **Last-write-wins for real conflicts** is acceptable to the authors as long as it's deterministic and users can fix the result afterwards.
- **Reuse the test suite.** The paper's scenarios (Examples 1–8) make good acceptance tests for whichever library we pick.
- **Library status:** the paper says the authors hope to fold Peritext into Automerge, and it names Yjs's rich-text approach as anomalous *as of 2022*. Both may have changed since. We need to check current versions before choosing.

steps.text:
I've read both papers in full and written a summary of each in a new Notes folder.

- **Notes/Local-first software — summary.** The problem is that cloud apps give you collaboration but take away ownership, and desktop apps do the opposite. The paper proposes "local-first" software: the copy on your device is the real one, and servers keep backup copies. It sets seven goals (fast, works across devices, works offline, collaborative, long-lasting, private, user-controlled) and scores existing tools against them. It puts forward CRDTs, data structures that let separate copies merge automatically, as the way to get there. The authors' prototype apps found that merging and offline use worked well and that conflicts were rarer than expected. The problems were edit history growing without limit, unreliable peer-to-peer networking, and the need for servers as helpers rather than the source of truth.
- **Notes/Peritext — summary.** The problem is that existing ways of merging rich text produce wrong results: duplicated words, bold spreading to the end of the document, comments splitting in two. The paper proposes a set of example scenarios that define a correct merge, and two settings for each kind of formatting: whether it can overlap with itself, and whether it grows when you type at its edge. It then describes Peritext, which stores formatting separately from the text, tied to the characters themselves rather than their positions, and proves every copy ends up the same. It handles only formatting within a paragraph: no headings, lists or other block elements yet.

Each summary ends with a section on what matters for adding real-time collaboration to the editor. Those points are my interpretation, and I've labelled them that way. The three most important:

1. **We need to decide what gets synced: the raw `.md` text or a structured document model.** If it's the raw text, Peritext doesn't apply. But Markdown's formatting symbols (`**`, `_`) would then behave like the hidden start/end markers the paper shows failing, so two people formatting overlapping text at once could leave broken markup. That's my inference; the paper doesn't test Markdown. Do you know which approach the editor uses or is heading toward?
2. **Markdown is mostly blocks** (headings, lists, quotes, code fences, tables), and Peritext doesn't cover them. We'll need a separate plan for those either way.
3. **Edit history grows without limit**, a problem both papers raise. Storage and cleanup of history should be planned from the start.

Both papers are from 2019 and 2022, so things they describe as unfinished may have changed since: Automerge's readiness, Yjs's handling of formatting, Peritext being added to Automerge. I didn't check current versions. I can look them up if that would help you choose a library.

args.path: Notes/Yjs vs Automerge for rich text — current state
args.content:
Web research on where the two main CRDT libraries stand for rich text, for an editor built on **ProseMirror** that **saves documents as Markdown**. Follows on from the Peritext and Local-first summaries in this folder.

Unless marked *(my reading)*, every point comes from the linked page. Some pages show no year, so check dates again before deciding.

## Short answers

- **Did Automerge adopt Peritext?** Yes. Rich text shipped in **Automerge 2.2**. Inline formatting uses Peritext-style marks stored outside the text, each with an "expand" setting. Blocks were added on top, using extensions to Peritext proposed by Martin Kleppmann.
- **Does Automerge handle blocks?** Yes. Block markers sit inline in the text, and each one has a type and a list of parents, which gives nesting. The built-in schema covers paragraph, heading (levels 1–6), code block, blockquote, ordered and unordered list items, and image.
- **Does Yjs handle blocks?** Yes, but as a tree. The stable binding `y-prosemirror` maps the document to a `Y.XmlFragment`. Its own caveats say splitting, merging and lifting nodes have no direct representation in Yjs, and Automerge shows an example where this loses text. A rewritten v2 binding is in pre-release.

## Automerge

**What shipped**
- Automerge 2.2 added rich text, with ProseMirror as the first editor it officially supports. — [Automerge 2.2: Rich Text](https://automerge.org/blog/rich-text/)
- Ink & Switch's May 2024 newsletter: Peritext covered only inline formatting, Kleppmann proposed extensions for blocks, and maintainer Alex Good implemented both in Automerge. — [Ink & Switch Dispatch 004 (May 2024)](https://www.inkandswitch.com/newsletter/dispatch-004/)
- The model is plain text with two additions:
  - **Marks** have a name, a primitive value and an `expand` option, so bold can grow at its edges and links don't.
  - **Block markers** sit in the text itself, and the text from one marker to the next is that block. — [Rich Text reference](https://automerge.org/docs/reference/documents/rich-text/)
- **Nesting** works through each block's `parents` array (e.g. a paragraph with parents `["blockquote", "ordered-list-item"]`). If a parent doesn't exist, it is created implicitly. By the docs' account, deleting a container or one of its sibling blocks therefore can't leave the blocks inside it orphaned. — [Rich Text Schema](https://automerge.org/docs/reference/under-the-hood/rich-text-schema/)
- **Built-in schema:**
  - marks: `strong`, `em`, `link`
  - blocks: `paragraph`, `heading`, `code-block`, `blockquote`, `ordered-list-item`, `unordered-list-item`, `image`
  - Anything else must be an application-specific `__ext__…` mark or block, and unknown ones should pass through untouched. The schema page calls itself "extremely minimal" and "a work in progress". — [Rich Text Schema](https://automerge.org/docs/reference/under-the-hood/rich-text-schema/)
- The authors say a detailed write-up of the block algorithm will come in a "future paper". I didn't find one. — [Automerge 2.2 blog](https://automerge.org/blog/rich-text/)

**ProseMirror binding (`@automerge/prosemirror`)**
- The README calls it **beta**: it has known bugs, and its API will change before a stable release. When I read it, the repo had 22 open issues and nearly all commits came from one contributor. — [automerge/automerge-prosemirror](https://github.com/automerge/automerge-prosemirror)
- Not every ProseMirror schema will do: it has to be one that Automerge's rich text can represent. The mapping is done with a `SchemaAdapter`: an `automerge` key on each node or mark spec, with a `within` option for list items and attribute parsers for heading level, link href and so on. You also have to define an `unknownBlock` node. — same page
- The editor starts from what Automerge holds, never the reverse. — same page
- `Automerge.updateSpans` updates block structure from a span list but leaves formatting alone for now. — [Rich Text reference](https://automerge.org/docs/reference/documents/rich-text/)

**Related:** Ink & Switch say their in-house **Markdown** editor, *Tiny Essay*, is built on Automerge. They used it to try out branches, grouped edits and a timeline of a document's history. The newsletter doesn't say how Tiny Essay stores Markdown. — [Dispatch 004](https://www.inkandswitch.com/newsletter/dispatch-004/)

## Yjs

**Stable binding (`y-prosemirror` 1.x)**
- It maps a `Y.XmlFragment`, a tree, to ProseMirror state. Features: syncing, shared cursors, per-user undo/redo, and recovery when concurrent edits leave a document its schema would reject. — [y-prosemirror README](https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror/blob/master/README.md)
- This is the most widely used route. Tiptap's collaboration extension builds on it (the README links to it). — same page

**Known issues relevant to us**
- **Concurrent structural edits.** Automerge's blog shows a y-prosemirror case where one user adds a list item while another converts the list to a paragraph, and the added item disappears. Automerge calls this "very rare" in live editing but "much more likely" after long offline sessions. — [Automerge 2.2 blog](https://automerge.org/blog/rich-text/) *(This is a competitor's description; the Yjs caveats below are consistent with it.)*
- **The Yjs maintainers' own caveats** (CAVEATS.md on master):
  - Yjs has no operation of its own for splitting, merging or lifting. A paragraph split is stored as "delete the tail, insert a new node", so ProseMirror positions can drift between peers. Comments, cursors and decorations should use Yjs relative positions instead.
  - Strict ProseMirror content rules (`+`, `{n,m}`) can become invalid under concurrent edits. The binding then deletes the parent node. The doc singles out offline users as the riskiest case and advises using `*` instead of `+` in schemas.
  - The maintainers considered flattening the document the way Automerge does. They decided against it for now because it would tie how documents are stored to ProseMirror's schema, and they want other tools, language models among them, to change the Yjs document without going through ProseMirror.
  - — [y-prosemirror CAVEATS.md](https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror/blob/master/CAVEATS.md)
- **Overlapping marks of the same type** (e.g. two comments on the same text):
  - An open Yjs bug from 2022 reports that overlapping same-type formatting loses information on sync. — [yjs/yjs#382](https://github.com/yjs/yjs/issues/382)
  - A 2020 y-prosemirror issue: two `comment` marks collapse into one. — [y-prosemirror#34](https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror/issues/34)
  - The new binding works around this by adding a hash suffix to each mark name. — [CAVEATS.md](https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror/blob/master/CAVEATS.md)
- I found nothing showing that Yjs has changed the start/end-marker formatting approach that the Peritext paper criticised. I also found nothing showing it hasn't. **Open:** test the paper's Examples 2–5 against current Yjs.

**v2 binding in progress**
- The releases page lists `v2.0.0-15` and earlier v2.0.0 pre-releases. The page shows dates without a year. — [y-prosemirror releases](https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror/releases)
- According to CAVEATS.md, the new binding:
  - isn't yet update-compatible with documents from the old binding (a migration is "planned")
  - adds attribution/suggestion rendering
  - is designed around upcoming **Yjs v14** schemas
  - — [CAVEATS.md](https://github.com/yjs/y-prosemirror/blob/master/CAVEATS.md)
- I couldn't confirm a Yjs v14 release date. The search hit a rate limit.

## Side by side

| | Automerge 2.2+ | Yjs + y-prosemirror |
|---|---|---|
| Inline marks | Peritext-style spans, per-mark `expand` | Formatting attributes on text; overlapping same-type marks are a known weak spot |
| Blocks | Flat block markers with `parents` for nesting | XML tree (`Y.XmlFragment`) |
| Split / merge / lift | Inserting or changing a block marker | Delete + insert; acknowledged limitation |
| ProseMirror binding maturity | Self-described beta | Stable 1.x in wide use; v2 in pre-release |
| Schema coupling | Schema must map onto the Automerge rich-text schema (extensible with `__ext__`) | Any ProseMirror schema; maintainers advise loosening `+` to `*` |
| Offline / long-divergence merges | Stated design goal | Maintainers flag offline as the riskier case |

## What this means for a ProseMirror + Markdown editor *(my reading)*

- **Neither library deals with Markdown.** Both sync a rich-text model, and Markdown is just our save format. We'd keep converting ProseMirror ↔ Markdown at load and save as we do now. The shared state would be the CRDT document, not the `.md` file. We still need to decide where the CRDT state is stored alongside or instead of the `.md` file, and which one counts as the real copy (see the local-first note).
- **Automerge's built-in schema is close to Markdown's block set**: paragraphs, headings 1–6, code blocks with language, blockquotes, ordered/unordered lists, images. It has **no inline code mark, tables, horizontal rule or hard break**. If we support any of those, they'd have to be `__ext__` types. *Open:* check whether the ProseMirror binding handles `__ext__` types well.
- **Comments:** Automerge mark values are primitives. I didn't find anything saying whether two same-name marks with different values (two comments) can overlap the way Peritext's comment model needs. Yjs has known problems here. *Open for both.*
- **If people mostly edit together live,** Yjs is the lower-risk and more mature option. The structural-merge problems mostly show up with concurrent block edits.
- **If we want long offline sessions or branch-and-merge,** Automerge's block model is designed for that. But its binding is beta, and we'd have to fit our ProseMirror schema to its mapping.
- **Whichever we pick,** the Peritext paper's Examples 1–8, plus a few block cases (concurrent list-item add vs list→paragraph, concurrent split of the same paragraph), make a useful acceptance test.

## Still to check

- Yjs v14 and y-prosemirror v2: release status and dates.
- Whether a paper on Automerge's block algorithm has been published since the 2.2 announcement.
- Current open issues on automerge-prosemirror that affect lists, headings and code blocks.
- How Tiny Essay stores Markdown in Automerge.

steps.text:
I've written up the research in **Notes/Yjs vs Automerge for rich text — current state**, with links throughout. Short version:

**Did Automerge take up Peritext?** Yes. Rich text shipped in Automerge 2.2. Formatting is stored the way Peritext describes, separately from the text, with a setting for whether it grows when you type at its edge. Automerge also added headings, lists and other blocks, based on extensions to Peritext proposed by Martin Kleppmann. There's an official ProseMirror binding, but its README calls it **beta**, with known bugs and an API that will change.

**Blocks:**
- **Automerge:** each block is a marker in the text with a type and a list of the blocks it sits inside, which is how nesting works. The built-in types are paragraph, heading 1–6, code block, blockquote, numbered and bulleted list items, and image. There's no inline code, table, horizontal rule or line break, so we'd have to add those as custom types.
- **Yjs:** `y-prosemirror` is stable and widely used, and stores the document as a tree. Its own maintainers' notes say splitting, joining and un-nesting blocks aren't directly supported. Concurrent edits can produce a document ProseMirror won't accept, and the binding then deletes the containing block; they single out offline users as the riskiest case. Automerge's blog shows a case in Yjs where a list item gets lost. A rewrite of the binding is in pre-release and isn't compatible with documents made by the current one yet.
- **Overlapping marks of the same type** (two comments on one passage) are a known problem in Yjs; a bug report about it from 2022 is still open. For Automerge I couldn't find out whether two overlapping comments work.

**For our setup:** neither library deals with Markdown. Both sync a rich-text document, so we'd keep converting ProseMirror ↔ Markdown when loading and saving, and decide which copy is the real one. My take: Yjs is the safer, more mature choice if people mostly edit together live. Automerge's way of handling blocks suits long offline sessions or branch-and-merge better, but its binding is still beta.

**Gaps:** the search tool hit a rate limit partway through. I couldn't confirm when the next major Yjs version (v14) or the rewritten ProseMirror binding will be released; the releases page shows dates without a year. I also didn't find whether Yjs has fixed the formatting problems the Peritext paper found. These are listed under "Still to check" at the end of the note.

say: Now write a design doc for adding real-time collaboration to the editor, in a Design folder: the problem, the options, a recommendation, and the risks. Base it on the notes, and say which note each point comes from. Keep it under 1,500 words.

args.content:
**Status:** Draft for discussion

**Sources:** each point is tagged with the note it comes from:
- **[LF]** Notes/Local-first software — summary
- **[PT]** Notes/Peritext — summary
- **[CS]** Notes/Yjs vs Automerge for rich text — current state
- **[Team]** what the team has told me about our editor: it is built on ProseMirror and saves documents as Markdown.

Points marked *(recommendation)* are my judgement and don't come from any source.

## 1. Problem

We want several people to be able to edit the same document at once, with each person's changes appearing for the others as they type. The editor is ProseMirror and documents are saved as Markdown [Team].

The difficulty is merging edits that happen at the same time:

- **Locking or "conflicted copy" files are the failure case.** Dropbox, Evernote and Git all make users merge by hand. Users now expect Google Docs-style automatic merging [LF].
- **Rich text is harder to merge than plain text.** Formatting can come out wrong in several ways [PT]:
  - Generic tree approaches can duplicate text when two people format the same words.
  - Hidden start/end markers can leave the rest of a document bold.
  - Formatting stored per character can split a comment in two.
- **Markdown is mostly block structure:** headings, lists, quotes, code fences, tables. Peritext doesn't cover blocks at all [PT]. Concurrent block edits (split, join, nest) are where current libraries are weakest [CS].
- **Offline is the hard case.** Live collaboration is the easy path. A long offline session followed by a merge is the real test [LF], and it's where library maintainers report the most risk [CS].

### Requirements

What the sources support:

1. Concurrent edits merge automatically. Every copy ends up the same, with no manual merging in normal use [LF, PT].
2. Inline formatting merges according to the Peritext rules. In particular, bold and italic expand when you type at their edge and links and comments don't, and overlapping comments are all kept [PT].
3. Block edits (headings, lists, quotes, code blocks) merge without losing text [CS].
4. The saved `.md` file stays readable by other tools [LF].
5. Edit history stays a manageable size [LF, PT].

**Not yet decided:** do we need long offline editing or branch-and-merge, or only live editing? This choice drives the recommendation (§3). Nothing in the notes answers it.

## 2. Options

### 2.1 What gets synced

**A. Sync the raw Markdown text with a plain-text CRDT.**
- Simple, and the file is the shared state.
- Formatting then lives as inline syntax (`**`, `_`, `[]()`). That is close to the control-character approach Peritext shows failing [PT]. This is my inference; the paper doesn't test Markdown. Concurrent formatting could leave stray or mismatched markers. Users can at least see and fix them [PT].
- It wastes ProseMirror's structured model.

**B. Sync the ProseMirror document through a rich-text CRDT, and keep Markdown as the save format.**
- Neither Yjs nor Automerge deals with Markdown. Both sync a rich-text model [CS].
- We keep converting ProseMirror ↔ Markdown on load and save, as now [CS, Team].
- We must decide where the CRDT state is stored and whether it or the `.md` file is the primary copy [LF, CS].

*(Recommendation)* **Option B.** Option A brings back the exact failure mode the Peritext paper documents, and doesn't use the editor we already have.

### 2.2 Which library

**Yjs + `y-prosemirror`** [CS]
- Stable 1.x binding in wide use, which Tiptap's collaboration extension builds on. Shared cursors and per-user undo/redo are built in.
- Stores the document as a tree (`Y.XmlFragment`). Yjs has no operation of its own for splitting, merging or lifting blocks. A split is stored as delete-then-insert, so ProseMirror positions can drift between peers.
- If concurrent edits produce a document the schema won't accept, the binding deletes the containing block. The maintainers single out offline users as the riskiest case and advise using `*` instead of `+` in schemas.
- Automerge's blog shows a case where a concurrent list-item add and list-to-paragraph change loses text. Automerge calls this rare in live editing but more likely after long offline sessions.
- Overlapping marks of the same type (two comments) are a known weak spot: an open 2022 bug, and a workaround in the new binding.
- A v2 binding is in pre-release and isn't yet compatible with v1 documents.
- I found no evidence on whether Yjs still shows the formatting anomalies the Peritext paper describes [CS, PT].

**Automerge 2.2+ + `@automerge/prosemirror`** [CS]
- Inline marks follow Peritext, each with an `expand` setting.
- Blocks are inline markers with a `parents` list for nesting. Splitting is just inserting a marker. A missing parent is recreated implicitly, so deleting a container can't orphan its children.
- Long offline divergence is an explicit design goal. Ink & Switch's own Markdown editor (Tiny Essay) is built on it.
- The binding calls itself **beta, with known bugs**, and almost all commits come from one maintainer.
- Our ProseMirror schema must map onto Automerge's schema through a `SchemaAdapter`. The built-in schema has no inline code, tables, horizontal rule or hard break, so those would be custom `__ext__` types.
- No paper on the block algorithm yet.

**Server-mediated OT** (`prosemirror-collab`, ShareDB) [LF, PT, CS]
- Proven for live editing. Google Docs, CKEditor and ProseMirror's own collab module use OT [PT].
- Needs a central server. Long offline sessions are slow to merge and branching isn't supported [PT].
- `prosemirror-collab` silently drops local steps that no longer apply cleanly, so an offline user can see a long stretch of their work disappear without warning [CS].
- Ruled out if offline matters. A fallback if it doesn't.

### 2.3 Network topology

- Peer-to-peer was far from ready for production in Ink & Switch's prototypes; NAT traversal was unreliable [LF].
- A server acting as a "cloud peer" relays and stores documents. It solves the problem of a collaborator being offline when you share, without becoming the source of truth [LF].
- CRDTs work fine over a server [LF].

*(Recommendation)* Use a sync/relay server in either case.

## 3. Recommendation *(recommendation)*

1. **Sync the ProseMirror document with a CRDT (Option B), and keep Markdown as import/export.** Treat the `.md` file as an export, not the shared state.
2. **Use a relay server, not peer-to-peer** [LF].
3. **Pick the library based on the offline requirement in §1:**
   - **Live editing only:** choose **Yjs**. It is mature. Its structural-merge problems are rare when everyone is online [CS], and we can reduce them by loosening our schema (`*` not `+`) [CS].
   - **Long offline sessions or branching are required:** choose **Automerge**. Its block model is built for this [CS]. We'd accept a beta binding and fit our schema to its mapping.
4. **Before committing, run both libraries against an acceptance suite.** The suite should contain:
   - Peritext Examples 1–8 [PT]
   - concurrent list-item add vs list→paragraph [CS]
   - concurrent splits of the same paragraph
   - overlapping comments [PT, CS]
   - a Markdown round-trip of every node type we support

   If the chosen library fails cases we care about, revisit the choice.
5. **Configure each mark using Peritext's two settings, overlap and expand** [PT]:
   - strong and emphasis: expand, don't overlap
   - links: don't expand, don't overlap
   - comments: don't expand, can overlap
   - inline code: our decision (not covered by the sources)
6. **Make incoming changes visible.** Show remote changes as they arrive and plan a history view [LF]. This matters more with any offline support.

## 4. Risks

| Risk | Source | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrent block edits lose text (Yjs) | [CS] | Loosen schema; acceptance tests; prefer Automerge if offline is needed |
| Schema-invalid merges delete parent blocks (Yjs, also `prosemirror-collab`) | [CS] | `*` over `+`; relaxed "invalid" node variants, as the y-prosemirror caveats suggest |
| Beta binding, single maintainer (Automerge) | [CS] | Acceptance tests; budget for fixing or forking the binding |
| Our schema doesn't fit Automerge's (tables, inline code, etc.) | [CS] | Map to `__ext__` types; check how the binding handles them (still open) |
| Overlapping comments collapse | [PT, CS] | Test early; store comment bodies separately, as Peritext suggests [PT] |
| Markdown round-trip loses information the CRDT holds (e.g. overlapping comments have no Markdown form) | My inference from [PT, CS] | Store comments outside the `.md`; decide which copy is primary |
| History grows without limit | [LF, PT] | Compaction or a compressed format from the start; Peritext cites under 1 byte per operation in Automerge's format [PT] |
| Users confused by changes arriving unseen | [LF] | Change highlighting and a history view |
| Yjs v2 binding migration: v1 documents not yet compatible | [CS] | If we choose Yjs, decide whether to start on v1 or v2 |
| Library facts go stale (some pages undated, research partly cut short by a rate limit) | [CS] | Re-check the "Still to check" list in [CS] before deciding |

## 5. Open questions

- Do we need long offline editing or branching? (Decides §3.3.)
- Where does the CRDT state live, and is it or the `.md` file the primary copy? [LF, CS]
- Sharing and permissions: what does "stop sharing" mean once a copy exists? [LF]
- Should the server see plaintext, or should we use end-to-end encryption? [LF]
- How do we keep clients running different app versions compatible? [LF]
- Release status of Yjs v14 / y-prosemirror v2. Is there a paper on Automerge's block algorithm? [CS]

I've worked through all three comments, and each one is resolved.

**1. Offline is required.**
- Offline editing for days at a time is now requirement 6 in §1, replacing the "Not yet decided" line.
- The recommendation now picks **Automerge**. The branch that would have chosen Yjs for live-only editing is gone.
- I also updated the places that depended on that choice: the server-based option (OT) is marked as ruled out, the first risk row now gives offline as the reason for choosing Automerge, and the old offline question is gone from the open questions.

**2. The least server we can get away with.** I added an assessment to §2.3. From least of our own infrastructure to most:
- **No server.** Sync the documents' collaboration state through Dropbox or iCloud, which people already use. The Local-first note supports this channel, but it isn't real-time. Dropbox-style tools also create conflicted copies, so the app would have to merge those itself. That's my inference; neither note tests it.
- **A hosted service someone else runs.** The notes name Pusher and Ably for live messaging and Firebase and CloudKit for hosted sync. **They don't say whether any of these work with Automerge.**
- **Peer-to-peer only.** This won't work for us. Besides being unreliable, it can't hold changes for someone who is offline for days, and your users will often not be online at the same time.

The recommendation is now: use a hosted relay or store if one works with Automerge, and fall back to file sync otherwise (offline drafting still works, but nothing is live). The doc's main goal is real-time collaboration, and the fallback gives that up, so finding a hosted option matters. I've added that question to Open questions and a risk row for the case where none turns up.

**3. Changes visible → Later.** The item is now in a new **§6 Later** at the end. I changed the matching risk row to say it's accepted for the first version and points to §6.

The doc is now about 1,650 words by my estimate, over your 1,500 limit, mostly because of the server options. I can trim it if you'd like; the library comparison in §2.2 is the easiest place to cut.

steps.text:
I re-read the current version first. Here's the review; I haven't changed anything.

## Overall

The doc is clear about what's sourced and what isn't. But the central decision rests on weaker evidence than the doc admits, and two of its own sections contradict each other. A sceptical reviewer would send it back on three points:

1. It promises real-time collaboration, but the fallback isn't real-time.
2. It picks Automerge before the test that is supposed to decide between the libraries.
3. It defers the one feature that makes days-long offline merges usable.

## Main weaknesses

**1. The fallback abandons the goal.** §1 says changes should appear "as they type". §3.2 says that if no hosted service works, we sync through Dropbox or iCloud, which "isn't real-time". That would be a different product: offline sync with merging. If file sync is an acceptable outcome, the problem statement should say so. If it isn't, the fallback should go.

**2. The library is chosen before the test.** §3.3 says "Choose Automerge". §3.4 then says "Before committing, run both libraries against an acceptance suite". One of these has to give. Either the suite decides the choice, or the choice is made and the suite only checks it.

**3. The evidence is lopsided.** Almost everything against Yjs comes from its maintainers' own candid list of known problems (their CAVEATS file). Almost everything for Automerge comes from its own announcement blog, its docs and its README. The CS note itself warns that the list-item loss example is "a competitor's description". The doc never says this. We haven't read anything comparable to the Yjs caveats for Automerge: neither its 22 open issues nor any independent reports. Its block-merging algorithm is unpublished ("No paper on the block algorithm yet"), so "Concurrent block edits lose text (Yjs) → The reason we chose Automerge" assumes Automerge doesn't have block-merge failures of its own. We don't know that.

**4. The chosen library may not meet requirement 2.** Requirement 2 and §3.5 need comments to overlap. The CS note says it's unknown whether Automerge can hold two overlapping marks of the same name, because mark values are primitives. So the recommendation picks a library without knowing whether it can meet one of the doc's own requirements. This should be a blocking test, not a row in the risks table.

**5. Deferring change visibility conflicts with the offline requirement.** You asked for this move, and that's your call. But here's why a reviewer would push back:
- Both papers say asynchronous collaboration needs a way to see what changed. LF says seeing a document's history matters. PT: a full async solution needs history and diff visualisation.
- Peritext keeps what each edit did, not what the writer meant by it.
- The LF finding that "conflicts are rarer than feared" came from informal testing (five team members and about ten outside users), mostly editing live. It says nothing about two people redrafting the same section on separate trains for three days.
- After that kind of merge, the text can interleave into nonsense with nothing to show the user what happened.

At minimum, the risks table should say this plainly, not file it as "users confused".

**6. The history-growth mitigation contradicts the note it cites.** "Compaction… from the start" sounds easy. The LF note says history "can't easily be dropped because a peer might reconnect months later", and that it caused real performance problems in Ink & Switch's PushPin prototype. Days of offline typing makes this worse. The only concrete figure (under 1 byte per operation) covers storage, not memory or load time.

**7. The doc both decides and doesn't decide which copy is primary.** §3.1 says "Treat the `.md` file as an export". §5 still lists "is it or the `.md` file the primary copy?" as open. Pick one.

## What's missing

**Existing documents and the load path.** The CS note says the ProseMirror document has to be built from the Automerge document, not the other way round. So "keep converting as now" isn't accurate: opening a `.md` file becomes "import into Automerge". The doc doesn't say:
- who does that import, or when;
- what happens if two people import the same file separately. My inference: that would produce two documents with unrelated histories that probably can't be merged;
- what happens to edits made to the `.md` in other tools. Requirement 4 says readable, but people will also write to it.

**Document identity and sharing.** There's no account of how a collaborator joins a document. LF suggests URLs and says permissions beyond secret URLs are unsolved. The doc lists permissions as an open question but proposes nothing for v1.

**Presence, cursors and undo.** The Yjs entry lists shared cursors and per-user undo/redo. The notes say nothing about either for Automerge's binding. If the comparison mentions them for one library, it needs to cover them for the other, and v1 should say whether it needs them.

**Behaviour under schema conflicts in Automerge.** The risk row says schema-invalid merges delete parent blocks "(Yjs, also `prosemirror-collab`)". The notes don't say what Automerge's binding does when a merged block structure doesn't fit our ProseMirror schema.

**Testing beyond the scenario list.** The Peritext authors also ran randomised testing: 5,000+ operations across three peers [PT]. With a beta binding, that matters more than a handful of hand-written cases.

**Scale, effort and success criteria.** The doc says nothing about document sizes, number of collaborators, how long a merge after days offline may take, or what makes v1 a success. The only effort signals are "budget for fixing or forking the binding" with no number, and CKEditor's reported 42 person-years [PT]. Those numbers have to come from you. The notes can't supply them, but a reviewer will ask.

## Claims not backed by the notes, or tagged to the wrong note

You asked for each point to be traced to a note. Several **[LF]** tags point to the original paper, not to my summary of it:
- The "sneakernet" over Dropbox and USB keys.
- Pusher and Ably. The LF note mentions only ShareDB.
- "Hosted sync scores low on privacy and longevity". The paper says this about Firebase; the note doesn't.

The facts are right; the tags are wrong. Either add these to the LF note or retag them to the paper.

Other unsupported or overstated points:
- **"Users can at least see and fix them [PT]"** (§2.1A). That was my own inference in the PT note, not the paper's claim. Tagging it [PT] passes my guess off as a source.
- **"What the sources support"** over the requirements. The requirements are design choices drawn from the sources. The Peritext paper calls its own rules "subjective".
- **"Concurrent block edits… are where current libraries are weakest [CS]"**. CS supports this for Yjs only.
- **"Tiny Essay is built on it"**, used as if it supported a Markdown workflow. The CS note says the newsletter "doesn't say how Tiny Essay stores Markdown".
- **Pusher and Ably as the hosted option.** These are message relays. As far as the notes go, nothing says they store documents for someone who is offline for days, and that storage is the whole reason §2.3 wants a server. *(My inference.)* Firebase and CloudKit can store documents, but the notes don't say whether they work with Automerge.
- **The risk "No hosted service fits Automerge"** is tagged [LF], but it's my inference. Its mitigation, "Check hosted options first (§5)", is a question, not a mitigation.
- **"Untagged opinion"**: "It wastes ProseMirror's structured model".

## Lead for the hosted-server question, from outside the notes

The automerge-prosemirror README I read during the research sets the editor up from a document handle obtained through a "repo" (`repo.find(...)`). That suggests Automerge has its own sync layer, which may be the best answer to "least server". I didn't write this into the CS note and haven't checked what it offers, so it's a lead, not a finding.

## Minor

- The doc is at 1,746 words against your 1,500 limit.
- The Yjs-only risk rows (v2 migration, schema `*` vs `+`) are left over from before the choice. Either keep them under a heading for the alternative or cut them.
- "(recommendation)" and "my inference" are used inconsistently. All of §3 is marked as recommendation, yet its items also cite sources.

If you want to fix these, I'd start with points 1–4 under Main weaknesses. They change the recommendation itself; the rest is cleanup.

I've fixed points 1, 2, 4 and 7 in the doc and left everything else as it was.

**1. The fallback that dropped real-time.** Dropbox/iCloud sync is no longer offered as a fallback. §2.3 now says it doesn't meet the real-time goal. §3.2 says to use a hosted relay or store if one works with Automerge. If none does, the team has to choose between running a minimal relay of our own and dropping live editing from v1. I didn't make that choice in the doc because it's a scope decision, so it's yours to make. I updated the matching row in the risks table too.

**2. Choosing the library before the test.** §3.3 now calls Automerge the leading candidate and says the acceptance tests make the final choice. If Automerge fails a blocking test, we try Yjs against the same tests. §3.4 now runs Automerge first and Yjs only if needed.

**4. Overlapping comments.** This is now the first test in §3.4 and is marked **blocking**: two comments on overlapping text must both survive a merge and a reload. The test explains why: the CS note leaves it open whether Automerge can do this, and Yjs has a known bug here. The risks table now points to it. Overlapping comments is the only test I marked blocking. The doc says the team decides which other cases block.

**7. Which copy is primary.** §3.1 now says plainly that the shared collaboration state (the CRDT) is the primary copy and the `.md` file is an export. §2.1B points to that decision, and the risks row about Markdown losing information now follows from it. In the open questions, "which copy is primary?" became "where is the CRDT state stored?", which is still undecided.
